facts.text: Watch the hospital hallway signs: they read "Farmacy" and "Phisical Therapy". Spelling wasn't a priority on this NYC set.
The psychiatrist talking to Emanuelle is played by director Joe D'Amato himself, in a cameo.
The film's alternate title, Trap Them and Kill Them, inspired the name of the American hardcore band Trap Them.
The end credits claim the jungle was shot in Tapurucuara, Brazil. It was actually a lake about 56 miles southeast of Rome.
The only real Amazon footage was lifted from the mondo film Porno Nights of the World (1977).
D'Amato admitted he was "a real copy-cat": Deodato's Last Cannibal World had been such a hit that he wanted to do something similar commercially.
Many cannibal extras were Filipinos living in Rome or visiting on vacation, rounded up and paid to work on set for a week.
The Italian Shock DVD trims a bit of dialogue in the cab scene around the 17-minute mark.
Make-up man Fabrizio Sforza recalls the shoot lasting two and a half weeks, "with effects, extras, violence, love scenes. Incredible!"
Sforza identifies the jungle lake as Lago di Fogliano, near Rome. Fogliano is also listed as a filming location.
Laura Gemser says D'Amato tried many times to get her to film hardcore scenes. She always gave him a resounding "No".
Gemser on the Emanuelle films: "It seemed like one long, long movie that didn't end." She kept going because they paid well and sent her to exotic places.
Gemser was born in Java, Indonesia. She is often wrongly called Dutch, a mix-up with Emmanuelle star Sylvia Kristel.
Gemser fell for co-star Gabriele Tinti on Black Emanuelle (1975). They married in New York a year later and stayed together until his death in 1991.
After leaving sex-symbol roles, Gemser turned to costume design, including the 1990 cult classic Troll 2.
Gabriele Tinti once guest-starred in the final episode of The Andy Griffith Show (1960s).
Nieves Navarro, also billed as Susan Scott, was an early spaghetti western actress, debuting in A Pistol for Ringo. She later became a giallo regular.
Donald O'Brien added "Donald" to his passport because credits kept misspelling his name and banks refused to cash his misspelled paychecks.
O'Brien started at Dublin's Gate Theatre. He credited Burt Lancaster with boosting his career on The Train (1964).
Percy Hogan was reportedly an American expat dancer living in Rome, according to Federico Fellini.
Unlike some earlier Black Emanuelle entries, this one has no hardcore sequences.
On the Italian Shock DVD, a shot of two men glancing at each other after the group finds a body under a blanket is cut, around the 49-minute mark.
The 2002 UK DVD lost 1 min 58 sec to the BBFC, trimming a rape scene, a gutting, and a breast-slicing close-up. Ontario's 1982 release was cut by 18 minutes.
In Germany it was released as Nackt unter Kannibalen, and the heroine was renamed Laura, after Gemser, to distance it from the Black Emanuelle series.
Many scenes were shot without proper permits.
The film's tagline: "That Emanuelle girl is back more EROTIC & EXOTIC than ever."
D'Amato's alias came from Silvio Amadio's L'isola delle svedesi (1969), where he worked as cinematographer. On set he used his real name, Aristide Massaccesi.
D'Amato's partner Fabrizio De Angelis co-produced this and Emanuelle and the White Slave Trade. They then split up their company, Fulvia Cinematografica.
D'Amato called the film "a reasonable commercial success, especially abroad."
The film plays NYC against Rome: the American Museum of Natural History, Roosevelt Island Tram and Rockefeller Plaza are listed as locations. The jungle was Italian.
The theme "Make Love on the Wing" was composed by Nico Fidenco and sung by Ulla Linder.
The Severin Blu-ray includes a 27-minute interview with composer Nico Fidenco and an 11-minute audio piece with the reclusive Laura Gemser.
The Monthly Film Bulletin called it "so preposterous as to be almost enjoyable."
Critic Danny Shipka found it "fairly harmless compared to other cannibal films," with the violence arriving in the last 20 minutes.
AllMovie's verdict: too gory for softcore fans and too dull for gorehounds, a film with "no target audience whatsoever."
Scout Tafoya called D'Amato "the Luchino Visconti of trash" in RogerEbert.com's video series The Unloved.
The film inspired The Green Inferno (2013) and is referenced in the 2015 Jungle Holocaust, among others.
Dread Central noted the film's "dubious distinction" of showing a penis being eaten less than 15 minutes after the opening credits.
Horror.Land listed this among its 2020 "Horror Films We Only Watch for the Nudity."
The credits say "This is a true story as reported by Jennifer O'Sullivan." It's not.
The Italian censors passed the film on 20 October 1977, visa #70973.
